title: +50% or -40%: a winning bet?
hook: A bet that gains 5% on average each round, played 100 times. Where do you end up?

knows: expected value of a simple bet
doesNotKnow: that compounding bets are judged by the typical (geometric) outcome, not the average
that a mean can be carried by a few lucky players

misconception: A bet with a positive expected return per round makes you richer over time.
objective: The learner can explain that with multiplying bets the typical player is governed by the product of factors (1.5 x 0.6 = 0.9 per head-tail pair), so most players shrink even though the average across players grows, carried by a few.

claims.text: The average round multiplies money by 1.05, a 5% gain: (1.5 + 0.6) / 2.
claims.source: Arithmetic mean of the two equally likely factors; meanFactor in src/demos/probability/plus-fifty-minus-forty/model.ts. Over 100 rounds the expected wealth is 1.05^100 = 131.5 times the start ($13,150 from $100).

claims.text: A head followed by a tail multiplies money by 0.9 (1.5 x 0.6); a typical player gets about 50 heads and 50 tails, so about 50 such pairs, and 0.9 fifty times leaves about half a percent of the start.
claims.source: 1.5 x 0.6 = 0.9; geometric mean sqrt(0.9) = 0.9487 (typicalFactor in model.ts).

claims.text: A player needs at least 56 heads in 100 rounds to end above the start, and only about 14% of players get them.
claims.source: 1.5^k x 0.6^(100-k) > 1 iff k > 55.75; P(Bin(100, 0.5) >= 56) = 0.1356 (headsToGain(), pAtLeast() in model.ts).

claims.text: The median player after 100 rounds holds about 0.5% of the start ($0.52 of $100).
claims.source: Median outcome has 50 heads and 50 tails: 0.9^50 = 0.00515 (medianAt() in model.ts).

claims.text: On the stage's first 50 players, the typical player ended at $1.29, 8 of 50 ended above $100, and the average of all 50 was $430.
claims.source: paths() in model.ts, seed 1505, untuned (the first seed tried). Over 500 other batches of 50: players above start ranged 1-14 (median 7), the batch median $0.08-$3.22 (middle 95%), and the batch average exceeded $100 in 82% of batches. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13 (revision v2): Was 'On the stage's first 50 players, the typical player ended at $1.29, 8 of 50 ended above $100, and their average was $430.' (fact-checker wording note: 'their average' could be read as the average of the 8 winners) | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Re-ran paths()/stats() in node (seed 1505): median 1.288 -> $1.29, 8 of 50 above $100, mean 429.76 -> $430 (the average of all 50). Over batches 1-500 (my own run): players above start 1-14 (median 7); batch mean exceeded $100 in 78.6%. The wording now says 'the average of all 50' so it cannot be read as the winners' average.

claims.text: This is a toy bet chosen to separate the average from the typical outcome.
claims.source: O. Peters (2019), The ergodicity problem in economics, Nature Physics 15: 1216-1221 (uses this coin game).

claims.text: A head then a tail turns $100 into $150 and then $90, a loss though heads and tails are equally likely; 'typical player' means the median (half the players end with less); each gridline on the stage is 100 times the one below.
claims.source: 100 x 1.5 = 150; 150 x 0.6 = 90 (UP, DOWN in model.ts); median = the middle of the 50 players' wealth (stats() in model.ts); axis ticks 0.01, 1, 100, 10,000, 1,000,000. Added by the builder 2026-10-13 in revision v2; needs an independent check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): 100 x 1.5 = 150, 150 x 0.6 = 90 (node); median in stats() is the mean of the two middle of 50 sorted wealths; gridlines at $0.01, $1, $100, $10,000, $1,000,000 are each 100x the one below (Demo.tsx line 36 and stage text). Also checked in node: 56+ heads in 100 needed to end ahead, P = 13.6%; expected wealth 100 x 1.05^100 = $13,150.

claims.text: Falling from $100 to $1 is a 99% loss.

recall.question: A fund gains 60% in good years and loses 50% in bad years, equally often. Its average year is +5%. What happens to a typical investor over 20 years?
recall.why: A good year and a bad year multiply money by 1.6 x 0.5 = 0.8. The typical path has as many good as bad years, so it shrinks, even though the average over all investors grows.
